ev.ind_m_first_rain.text: After two months of blazing heat the monsoon finally broke. Children dance in the downpour, grown-ups stand in doorways silently breathing in the wet earth — it smells as if life is starting over.
ev.ind_m_holi.text: The spring festival of Holi: you were dusted head to toe with red and yellow powder and drenched with coloured water. Until evening you walked about as bright as a parrot, laughing with everyone.
ev.ind_m_diwali.text: On the night of Diwali every house set little clay oil lamps along its ledges. The whole street flickers, and you sat on the doorstep counting the flames until you lost count somewhere past three hundred.
ev.ind_m_eid.text: The fast is over: it is Eid. After the prayer everyone embraces, children in new clothes run from neighbour to neighbour for sweet rice pudding, and the poor at the mosque door receive more alms than all year long.
ev.ind_m_mango.text: Mango season has come. You ate so many ripe fruits that the juice ran down to your elbows. The poets call the mango the pride of Hindustan, and today you agree with them completely.
ev.ind_m_paan.text: After the meal you chew paan, a betel leaf wrapped around areca nut and a pinch of lime. Your lips turn red, your mouth feels fresh, and the talk with the neighbours stretches on till sunset.
ev.ind_m_storyteller.text: By the fire an old storyteller told how Rama went after Sita to the island of Lanka while the monkeys built a bridge across the sea. You listened until midnight and could not sleep for a long time after.
ev.ind_m_sand_letters.text: At the school under the tree the teacher had you trace letters with a finger on a board strewn with sand. One mistake, wipe it with your palm and start again. By evening your finger is sore, but you can write your name.
ev.ind_m_loo_roof.text: In May the scorching loo wind blows from the west, and no one goes out by day. At night the whole quarter sleeps on the flat roofs, on rope cots, talking to the neighbours across the lane.
ev.ind_m_qutb_minar.text: For the first time you saw the Qutb Minar up close, a tower of red stone ringed with carved inscriptions. You tipped your head back so far you nearly fell over: can people really have built this?
ev.ind_m_qawwali.text: In the evening at a Sufi saint's tomb the qawwals sang verses of love for God. Clapping, a drum, one voice catching up another. Beside you both Muslims and Hindus wept with joy.
ev.ind_m_hampi_bazaar.text: At the great bazaar by the temple pearls, rubies and diamonds are sold in heaps, like grain. Foreign merchants walk about open-mouthed. You begged a tiny chip of garnet as a gift and carry it like a treasure.
ev.ind_m_mahanavami.text: Nine nights of the Mahanavami festival. On a high stone platform the raya is saluted by hundreds of caparisoned elephants, dancers, wrestlers and troops. Fireworks burst over the city, and it seems the whole empire has gathered in one square.
ev.ind_m_hampi_ruins.text: You passed the ruins of the old capital. Grass grows in the empty halls, herdsmen drive goats past broken statues. The old people say there were once more people here than stars in the sky.
ev.ind_m_chilli.text: A merchant sells dried red pods brought by the firangis, the men from over the sea. You bit off a piece and wept for a long time, gulping water. But with them even plain gruel becomes a feast.
ev.ind_m_kolam.text: At dawn you draw a kolam at the doorstep, a pattern of rice flour. Ants and birds will have eaten it by noon, and that is as it should be: let the house feed the small creatures too.
ev.ind_m_muslin_ring.text: An old weaver showed you a trick: a whole length of muslin slipped through his finger ring. "They call cloth like this woven wind," he said, and laughed at your face.
ev.ind_m_hilsa.text: The rainy season is the season of hilsa. It is fried in mustard oil, and the smell drifts over the whole village. It is full of bones, but for that taste you can put up with them.
ev.ind_m_boat_song.text: You crossed the wide river by boat. All the way the boatman sang a long slow song about the river carrying everything away, sorrow and joy alike. The far bank was a long time coming out of the mist.
ev.ind_m_stepwell.text: In the heat everyone goes down into the stepwell: dozens of steps down to the cool water, past carved goddesses in their niches. At the bottom the women fill their pots and catch up on the whole week's news.
ev.ind_m_jain_monk.text: A Jain monk in white walked slowly down the street. Before each step he brushed the path with a soft whisk so as not to crush a single ant. You watched him for a long while.
ev.ind_m_dhow_harbor.text: At the harbour hot-blooded horses are led down the gangplank of an Arab ship, while porters carry bales of cotton and indigo into the hold. It smells of pitch, pepper and the sea. Somewhere beyond the horizon lie Aden and Hormuz.
ev.ind_m_wrestling.text: At dawn in the akhara, the wrestling pit, you watched the pahlwans rub themselves with oil and throw each other onto the soft earth. An old wrestler noticed you and let you try. You ended up on your back three times and did not regret it once.
ev.ind_m_chaupar.text: All evening you played chaupar: cowrie shells tossed onto the cloth, pieces racing round the cross-shaped board. You beat the grown-ups twice in a row, and now they suspect you of sorcery.
ev.ind_m_dung_floor.text: Every week you smear the earthen floor with a fresh mix of cow dung and clay. The floor turns smooth and cool, the flies leave, and the house smells clean, the village way.
ev.ind_m_jasmine.text: The flower seller wove you a jasmine garland for your hair. All evening a sweet scent followed you about, and even the grumpy neighbour said you looked lovely today.
ev.ind_m_henna.text: Before a friend's wedding all the women of the quarter gathered to paint her hands with henna. They painted a pattern on your palms too — you mustn't touch anything till morning, and everyone laughed, feeding each other by hand.
ev.ind_m_elephants_bath.text: At the river the mahouts were bathing the elephants, scrubbing their backs with bricks while the elephants sprayed them back from their trunks. You stood on the bank until one of the giants soaked you too.
ev.ind_m_caravan.text: All day a Banjara caravan passed the village: thousands of oxen carrying sacks of grain and salt. Dust rose to the sky, and the drovers sang and jingled their bangles.
ev.ind_m_sacred_thread.text: Today is your upanayana: the priest laid the sacred thread over your shoulder and whispered an ancient prayer in your ear. Now you are "twice-born" and must study. The thread tickles, but you may not take it off.
ev.ind_m_ramadan_heat.text: Ramadan has fallen in the hot months. Not a sip of water all day, and at sunset a date, a sip of sherbet and such bliss it seems you have never tasted anything better in your life.
ev.ind_m_first_tanka.text: For the first time you were allowed to hold a silver coin with a Persian inscription. You studied the letters you cannot read and wondered how many sweets it would buy.
ev.ind_m_firangi.text: You saw firangis for the first time, men from a Portuguese ship. Faces red from the sun, heavy coats in this heat, crosses round their necks. They say they sail here for a whole year around Africa.
ev.ind_m_mughal_garden.text: You were let into a garden laid out the Persian way: four squares, water channels, fountains and roses. They say Padishah Babur missed the gardens of Kabul and so ordered them built everywhere.
ev.ind_m_spice_smell.text: In the spice row of the bazaar there are mounds of turmeric, cumin and cardamom. You sneezed so loudly the trader burst out laughing and pressed a handful of sweet fennel seeds into your hand.
ev.ind_m_cotton_harvest.text: Cotton picking: the bolls have burst open and the field has turned white, as if dusted with snow. Your fingers are pricked, your back aches, and by evening fluff is floating over the whole village.
ev.ind_d_moneylender.title: The moneylender
ev.ind_d_moneylender.text: Sowing time is near and there is no money for seed or for an ox. The sahukar, the moneylender, will lend against an entry in his ledger — but his interest grows faster than rice.
ev.ind_t_debt_due.title: The debt has grown
ev.ind_t_debt_due.text: The sahukar came with his ledger: over the years the debt has almost doubled. He offers a choice — repay it all now, work it off for him, or hand over your best field.
ev.ind_d_jati_council.title: The jati council
ev.ind_d_jati_council.text: You shared a meal with a friend from another jati, and word got out. The council of your community's elders, the panchayat, has ruled that you must atone: feast the whole community and undergo a purification rite. Otherwise no one will eat with your family or marry into it.
ev.ind_d_jati_council.argue.success: You reminded them that this friend once saved your life in a flood. The elders whispered among themselves and settled for a prayer.
ev.ind_d_jati_council.argue.failure: The elders grew angry. Now the neighbours look away, and no one invites you to weddings.
ev.ind_d_pilgrimage.title: Pilgrimage
ev.ind_d_pilgrimage.text: The neighbours are setting out for Kashi, the holy city on the Ganges: to bathe in the river, bow before Shiva and come home purified. The road is long, the toll posts tax pilgrims, but people dream of this all their lives.
ev.ind_d_pilgrimage.text.vijayanagara: The neighbours are setting out on pilgrimage to the temple of Venkateshwara in the hills of Tirupati. The road is long and costly, but people dream of this all their lives.
ev.ind_d_pilgrimage.text.gujarat: The neighbours are setting out for Dwarka, Krishna's city at the edge of the sea. The road across the wastes is risky and costly, but people dream of this all their lives.
ev.ind_d_hajj.title: The hajj
ev.ind_d_hajj.text: Pilgrim ships sail from the harbours of Gujarat to Jeddah, and from there the road leads to Mecca. The sea, pirates, the desert heat... But to come home a hajji is an honour for life.
ev.ind_d_hajj.go.success: You walked around the Kaaba and came home a hajji. The neighbours met you at the gate.
ev.ind_d_hajj.go.failure: You reached Mecca, but on the way back a fever struck you down. You came home barely alive.
ev.ind_d_iqta.title: The iqta
ev.ind_d_iqta.text: The sultan grants you an iqta, the right to collect the revenue of several villages. In return you must keep a troop of horsemen for him and come at his first call.
ev.ind_d_iqta.note: The iqta was a conditional land assignment in the Delhi Sultanate: an amir drew the revenue of villages in return for military service. Iqtas were not hereditary, and sultans often moved their holders around so they would not put down roots.
ev.ind_t_iqta_recall.title: The farman
ev.ind_t_iqta_recall.text: A sealed farman has arrived: your iqta is being handed to another amir, and you are ordered to a distant province. Rumour says someone whispered to the sultan that you had grown too friendly with the local zamindars.
ev.ind_t_iqta_recall.bribe: Send a gift to the vizier
ev.ind_t_iqta_recall.bribe.success: The gift was well received. The farman was "lost", and you stayed where you were.
ev.ind_t_iqta_recall.bribe.failure: The vizier took the gift and took the iqta anyway.
ev.ind_d_jizya.title: Jizya
ev.ind_d_jizya.text: The collector demands the jizya, the poll tax on non-Muslims. This time he has assessed you at the top rate, as if you were rich, though your house holds nothing but mats.
ev.ind_d_jizya.note: The jizya was a poll tax on non-Muslims in Islamic states. In the Delhi Sultanate it was collected unevenly; Firuz Shah Tughluq extended it to brahmins as well. Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564.
ev.ind_d_jizya.plead.success: The neighbours vouched for you, and the collector grumbled and reassessed you at the lowest rate.
ev.ind_d_jizya.plead.failure: The collector decided you were hiding money and added a fine.
ev.ind_d_horse_trade.title: Horses from over the sea
ev.ind_d_horse_trade.text: The raya's army needs horses, and good horses are not bred in the hot Deccan. Arab and Persian chargers come by sea to the western ports, and the raya pays for each one as if for a village. A partner urges you to invest in a shipment.
ev.ind_d_horse_trade.note: Vijayanagara bought thousands of warhorses from Arab, Persian and, after 1510, Portuguese merchants through the ports of the western coast. The horses fared badly in the local climate, so demand never dried up.
ev.ind_d_horse_trade.invest.success: The horses arrived alive, and the raya's stablemasters paid in gold.
ev.ind_d_horse_trade.invest.failure: Half the horses died on the way. Your partner just spreads his hands.
ev.ind_d_dargah_vow.title: A thread on the lattice
ev.ind_d_dargah_vow.text: Still no children in the house. The neighbours advise going to a Sufi saint's tomb and tying a thread to the carved stone lattice: Muslim and Hindu women alike do it, and when the wish comes true, the thread must be untied.
ev.ind_t_vow_child.title: The vow fulfilled
ev.ind_t_vow_child.text: A child has been born in the house! You went back to the saint's tomb, untied your thread and handed out sweets to the poor, as you had promised.
ev.ind_d_sati.title: Sati
ev.ind_d_sati.text: The master of a noble house next door has died. His widow has declared she will join him on the funeral pyre. Some speak of the highest devotion and bring her flowers; others weep quietly and look away.
ev.ind_d_sati.note: Sati, the self-immolation of a widow on the funeral pyre, was a rare but revered custom in some noble families, especially among Rajputs and in Vijayanagara. Many Indian thinkers and Muslim rulers condemned it, and Akbar forbade sati performed under compulsion.
ev.ind_d_sati.dissuade: Try to talk her family out of it
ev.ind_d_sati.dissuade.success: The family gave way: the widow will live and go on pilgrimage. Someone called you a troublemaker, but she thanked you with her eyes.
ev.ind_d_sati.dissuade.failure: No one would listen, and you were shown out of the gate. You cannot forget the smoke over the river.
ev.ind_d_widow.title: White garments
ev.ind_d_widow.text: You have been widowed. By the custom of the high jatis a widow wears white, eats plain food, gives up ornaments and festivals, and may not marry again. Your late husband's family expects you to stay in their house, near your child.
ev.ind_d_widow.return: Go back to your own kin
ev.ind_d_widow.devotion: Devote yourself to prayer and the temple
ev.ind_d_well_gift.title: A well by the road
ev.ind_d_well_gift.text: Drought after drought, and on the high road there is neither well nor tank. With your own money you could build a stepwell with a shelter for travellers — a meritorious deed, to be recorded in an inscription on stone.
ev.ind_d_well_gift.small: Give money to mend the old tank
ev.ind_t_well_blessing.title: Travellers' blessings
ev.ind_t_well_blessing.text: In a year of drought your well saved a whole village and more than one caravan. Travellers bless your name, and the stone inscribed with the donor's name still stands by the steps.
ev.ind_d_perpetual_lamp.title: The perpetual lamp
ev.ind_d_perpetual_lamp.text: The temple asks for a gift for a "perpetual lamp": a flock of sheep given to the temple herdsman, so that every day he brings ghee for the lamp before the deity. The donor's name will be carved on the temple wall, forever.
ev.ind_d_perpetual_lamp.note: Thousands of inscriptions on the walls of south Indian temples record gifts for a "perpetual lamp": donors gave the temple livestock or money, and with that income a ghee lamp burned day and night before the deity.
ev.ind_d_betrothal.title: Betrothal
ev.ind_d_betrothal.text: Neighbours from your jati propose to betroth {npc} to their child. The wedding will come later, when the children are grown; for now there are gifts to exchange, horoscopes to match, and the word of two families, which is never taken back.
ev.ind_d_betrothal.wait: Wait until the child is older
ev.ind_t_betrothal_wedding.title: A wedding long promised
ev.ind_t_betrothal_wedding.text: The time has come for the wedding agreed so many years ago. Drums, fire, seven steps around the sacred flame — {g=npc_sex:your son brings home his bride|your daughter leaves for her husband's house}. A great deal of money was spent, and even more tears.
ev.ind_d_persian.title: The language of power
ev.ind_d_persian.text: The teacher says: decrees, tax rolls and court poetry are all written in Persian. Whoever knows Persian will find a place in the chancery. But your elders want you to learn Sanskrit and the holy books — or simply to count money, like everyone in the family.
ev.ind_t_munshi_offer.title: A munshi wanted
ev.ind_t_munshi_offer.text: Your Persian has paid off: the governor needs a munshi, a secretary for letters, accounts and reports to court. Good pay, work late into the night.
ev.ind_d_sitala.title: Smallpox
ev.ind_d_sitala.text: {npc} is burning with fever and a rash has spread across the skin: smallpox. The neighbours whisper that the goddess Sitala has come visiting, and she must be appeased, not driven out. The vaidya will treat the illness, for a fee.
ev.ind_d_sitala.vaidya.success: Decoctions, cool neem leaves, rest. In two weeks the fever was gone.
ev.ind_d_sitala.vaidya.failure: The healer did all he could. Now there is only waiting and prayer.
ev.ind_d_sitala.goddess.success: You took an offering to the temple and never left the bedside. The illness retreated.
ev.ind_d_sitala.goddess.failure: The goddess did not listen. The days drag on in agony.
ev.ind_d_sitala.care.success: Sleepless nights, water, neem leaves. The fever broke, leaving only marks on the skin.
ev.ind_d_sitala.care.failure: You did not sleep for a week, but the illness was stronger.
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.title: Fever
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.text: For three days a fever has been shaking you: burning one moment, shivering the next. The vaidya offers bitter decoctions, oils and a strict diet. The neighbours say make a vow at a shrine. And the work won't wait.
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.vaidya.success: The vaidya felt your pulse, declared that the fire of pitta had flared in your body and prescribed bitter herbs. Within a week you were on your feet.
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.vaidya.failure: The potions are bitter and do little good. The illness lingers.
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.shrine: Make a vow at a shrine
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.shrine.success: You spent the night at the shrine, and by morning the fever had broken.
ev.ind_d_fever_cure.shrine.failure: The prayers did not help, and the journey only sapped your strength.
ev.ind_d_afim.title: Afim
ev.ind_d_afim.text: After a hard day a Rajput acquaintance offers you afim, opium dissolved in water. "It takes away pain and weariness. Every warrior takes it, and we welcome guests with it."
ev.ind_d_toddy.title: Palm wine
ev.ind_d_toddy.text: The palm tapper offers you toddy, palm sap that has fermented in a day of heat. After work in the fields it seems the best medicine in the world.
ev.ind_d_toddy.sometimes: Have a cup now and then
ev.ind_d_diwali_dice.title: Dice on Diwali night
ev.ind_d_diwali_dice.text: On Diwali night it is the custom to throw dice: they say whoever plays tonight will enjoy the goddess Lakshmi's favour all year. The stakes are rising, and the neighbours are flushed.
ev.ind_d_diwali_dice.big.success: The dice love you tonight! You leave with a full purse.
ev.ind_d_diwali_dice.big.failure: Lakshmi was looking the other way. You lost, and you are already thinking about winning it back.
ev.ind_d_boundary.title: The boundary stone
ev.ind_d_boundary.text: During the night your neighbour moved the boundary stone two paces onto your land. You could call the village elders, the panchayat; you could go to the judge in town; or you could settle it with a stick.
ev.ind_d_boundary.panchayat.success: The old men remembered where the stone stood in their grandfathers' day. The neighbour had to put it back and feast everyone.
ev.ind_d_boundary.panchayat.failure: The neighbour brought kinsmen as witnesses, and the elders decided to "split the dispute down the middle".
ev.ind_d_boundary.court: Go to the judge in town
ev.ind_d_boundary.court.success: An old entry turned up in the revenue register. The judge found in your favour.
ev.ind_d_boundary.court.failure: Clerks, fees, delays — and then a ruling against you.
ev.ind_d_boundary.fight.success: The neighbour lost his nerve and moved the stone back during the night.
ev.ind_d_boundary.fight.failure: The neighbour's sons turned out to be tougher. You are lying with a broken head.
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.title: The monsoon has failed
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.text: The monsoon never came. The rice has withered where it stood, the wells are shrinking, and grain prices at the bazaar climb every day. The old people remember the hungry years and shake their heads.
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.city: Go to the capital to find work
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.wait: Wait for grain to be handed out
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.wait.success: The governor opened the state granaries. The gruel was thin, but you lasted until the next harvest.
ev.ind_d_monsoon_fail.wait.failure: No grain came. The months of hunger were very hard.
ev.ind_d_temple_car.title: The god's chariot
ev.ind_d_temple_car.text: The chariot festival: thousands of people haul a huge wooden car bearing the deity's image down the street on thick ropes. To lay a hand on the rope earns great merit, but in the crush you can fall underfoot.
ev.ind_d_temple_car.pull.success: You pulled with everyone else, singing and weeping. You have never felt such oneness.
ev.ind_d_temple_car.pull.failure: The crowd surged and knocked you down. You got away with bruises, but you will remember the festival forever.
ev.ind_d_apprentice.title: What to teach
ev.ind_d_apprentice.text: It is time to teach {npc} a trade. By the custom of the jati the craft passes from elders to the young. But a master in the next quarter takes paying apprentices and promises to teach more, and a literate scribe offers reading and reckoning.
ev.ind_d_apprentice.school: Send to the scribe to learn letters
ev.ind_d_purdah.title: Behind the curtain
ev.ind_d_purdah.text: Women of your standing should not show their faces at the bazaar. But the silk merchant has cheated the servants again, and you want to choose the cloth yourself.
ev.ind_d_purdah.openly: Go yourself, under a light veil
ev.ind_tr_robbers.title: Fellow travellers
ev.ind_tr_robbers.text: On the road to the fair some travellers fell in with you: polite, pious, generous with stories. Then at night by the fire they all rose at once, and there were knives in their hands.
ev.ind_tr_robbers.fight.success: You grabbed a burning brand from the fire and charged. The robbers, expecting no resistance, fled into the dark.
ev.ind_tr_robbers.fight.failure: There were too many of them. You were beaten and stripped of everything.
ev.ind_tr_robbers.bargain.success: You handed over part of your money and convinced them there was nothing more.
ev.ind_tr_robbers.bargain.failure: They did not believe you. They searched you, took everything and beat you as well.
ev.ind_tr_captive.title: The raid
ev.ind_tr_captive.text: At dawn horsemen of a neighbouring ruler burst into the village. Houses are burning, cattle are driven off, and captives are tied with ropes to be sold at the slave market.
ev.ind_tr_captive.hide: Hide in the reeds by the river
ev.ind_tr_captive.hide.success: You stayed in the water until dark. The horsemen left behind nothing but ashes.
ev.ind_tr_captive.hide.failure: They found you. A rope around your neck, a long road, and the slave market.
ev.ind_tr_captive.fight.success: You and the neighbours held them off at the well. You are wounded, but free.
ev.ind_tr_captive.fight.failure: You were knocked down and bound. The slave market lies ahead.
ev.ind_t_ransom.title: Ransom
ev.ind_t_ransom.text: People from your home village tracked you down and gathered a ransom, a little from every household. The master counted the coins and signed your release. You can go back to the village, or stay in town and work off the debt to your neighbours.
ev.ind_t_ransom.repay: Stay in town and work it off
ev.ind_tr_ghulam.title: Ghulam
ev.ind_tr_ghulam.text: Your master, an amir, has noticed your wits and strength. His ghulams are taught to ride, to shoot the bow and even to write, and then they are led on campaign. They say many ghulams became commanders, and some even sultans.
ev.ind_tr_ghulam.note: Ghulams were military slaves bought, trained and promoted by Muslim rulers. Qutb al-Din Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban, founders of the Delhi Sultanate, all began as ghulams, which is why its first dynasty is often called the "Slave dynasty".
ev.ind_t_ghulam_freed.title: Freedom and a horse
ev.ind_t_ghulam_freed.text: After a victorious campaign your master freed you before everyone, gave you a horse and set you over a hundred riders. Yesterday's fellow ghulams now call you "sardar".
ev.ind_tr_royal_favor.title: The sovereign's favour
ev.ind_tr_royal_favor.text: Out hunting, you were beside the sovereign when a tiger startled his horse, and you caught the reins in time. A week later a messenger came: you are granted a governorship, a robe of honour and the revenue of a whole district.
ev.ind_tr_royal_favor.text.vijayanagara: Out hunting, you were beside the raya when a tiger startled his horse, and you caught the reins in time. A week later a messenger came: you are granted a nayaka's lands and the right to keep your own troops.
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.title: The envious
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.text: Rivals at court have whispered that you hold back revenue and secretly write to the sovereign's enemies. You are summoned to answer for it.
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.defend: Plead your case before the sovereign
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.defend.success: You brought the ledgers and witnesses. The slanderer himself was packed off to a distant fortress.
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.defend.failure: You were not believed. Your post and half your property were taken, leaving only your ancestral villages.
ev.ind_t_court_intrigue.pay: Win over the vizier with gifts
ev.ind_tr_treasure.title: A pot in the furrow
ev.ind_tr_treasure.text: The ploughshare clinked against a clay pot. Inside are old silver coins, black with age. By law a treasure belongs to the sovereign — but who would know?
ev.ind_t_treasure_informer.title: Informed on
ev.ind_t_treasure_informer.text: Someone informed on you about the treasure. The kotwal's men turned the house upside down, took everything they found and fined you on top of it.
ev.ind_tr_cargo.title: The ship does not return
ev.ind_tr_cargo.text: Your bales of cloth sailed for Malacca, and pepper and cloves were to come back. The time has passed, and there is no word. Another merchant offers to buy your share, at a third of its value.
ev.ind_tr_cargo.wait.success: The ship came in, riding low in the water. The profit is enough to buy a share in a ship of your own.
ev.ind_tr_cargo.wait.failure: Word came: the ship was wrecked off Ceylon. Everything is lost.
ev.ind_tr_false_theft.title: Accused
ev.ind_tr_false_theft.text: A rich neighbour's silver bangles have gone missing, and his servant swears he saw you by the gate. The kotwal, chief of the town watch, has already sent for you.
ev.ind_tr_false_theft.witnesses.success: Three respected men vouched for you, and the bangles later turned up with the servant himself.
ev.ind_tr_false_theft.witnesses.failure: The witnesses were not believed. You were flogged and made to pay for the bangles.
ev.ind_tr_elephant_rampage.title: An elephant in the bazaar
ev.ind_tr_elephant_rampage.text: A war elephant has broken its chain and is charging through the bazaar, sweeping stalls aside. Right in its path a small child in a silk shirt stands frozen.
ev.ind_tr_elephant_rampage.save.success: You snatched the little one from under the giant's very feet. The child turned out to be from a rich house; the family showered you with gifts and promised you their patronage.
ev.ind_tr_elephant_rampage.save.failure: You managed to push the child clear, but the elephant caught you. You lay for a long time with broken ribs.
ev.ind_tr_river_course.title: The river moved
ev.ind_tr_river_course.text: In a single rainy week the river changed its course: your field and half the village went under. But downstream a new char island has risen from the water — fresh silt, nobody's land.
ev.ind_tr_river_course.char: Claim land on the new island
ev.ind_tr_river_course.char.success: The silt was rich, and the very first rice harvest was splendid.
ev.ind_tr_river_course.char.failure: The next flood washed away half the island along with your crop.
ev.ind_tr_river_course.kin: Go to your kin in the next village
ev.ind_tr_renounce.title: The call of the road
ev.ind_tr_renounce.text: More and more often at night you think that home, money and worries are only a dream. A wandering ascetic by the river told you: "You have already left. All that remains is to stand up and go." Many men your age give away their property and go in search of God.
ev.ind_tr_renounce.go: Give it all away and go
ev.ind_j_musth.title: Musth
ev.ind_j_musth.text: Your elephant has gone into musth, the season of fury: dark fluid runs from his temples, he knows no one, strains at his chains and bellows at night. The master insists the elephant must walk in the procession next week.
ev.ind_j_musth.calm.success: You sat beside him for three nights, sang him old songs and fed him by hand. The elephant settled, and the master raised your pay.
ev.ind_j_musth.calm.failure: The elephant flung you aside with his trunk. You are lucky to be alive.
ev.ind_j_devadasi_festival.title: Dance before the deity
ev.ind_j_devadasi_festival.text: At the great festival you are invited to dance before the deity in the temple's main hall, before the nobles and perhaps the ruler himself. The senior dancers watch your every move jealously.
ev.ind_j_devadasi_festival.dance.success: The bells at your ankles rang in time with the drum, and the hall held its breath. By morning the whole city was talking about you.
ev.ind_j_devadasi_festival.dance.failure: You lost the rhythm at the most solemn moment. The senior dancers exchanged glances.
ev.ind_j_devadasi_festival.yield: Give way to a senior dancer
ev.ind_j_devadasi_patron.title: A patron
ev.ind_j_devadasi_patron.text: A rich merchant, a generous donor to the temple, offers you his patronage: a house, jewels, a comfortable life. Devadasis often had such patrons, but the temple and your teachers expect you to stay devoted above all to your service.
ev.ind_j_muslin_court.title: An order for the palace
ev.ind_j_muslin_court.text: The steward of the palace workshop orders a length of the finest muslin, "morning dew", for the sultan's court. The thread is so fine it can only be spun at dawn while the air is damp. A year's work.
ev.ind_j_muslin_court.take.success: The cloth turned out so light, they say, it could not be seen lying on the grass. You were paid generously, and now you have your own workshop with apprentices.
ev.ind_j_muslin_court.take.failure: Your eyes grow tired, the thread keeps breaking. The cloth was accepted, but only half paid for.
ev.ind_j_cartaz.title: Cartaz
ev.ind_j_cartaz.text: The Portuguese have declared themselves masters of the sea: any ship without their pass, the cartaz, may be seized and burned. The sealed paper must be bought at their fortress, and on the way back you must call there again and pay duty.
ev.ind_j_cartaz.note: From the early sixteenth century the Portuguese required Asian ships in the Indian Ocean to buy a pass, the cartaz, and pay duties at their fortresses. Ships without a cartaz were seized. Many Gujarati merchants paid; others sailed in convoys or took the risk.
ev.ind_j_cartaz.risk.success: You slipped out at night along the coast. Not a Portuguese sail in sight, and the goods sold at a profit.
ev.ind_j_cartaz.risk.failure: Portuguese ships appeared off the cape. The cargo was taken, the ship burned, and the crew barely let go.
ev.ind_j_spice_ship.title: A ship of your own
ev.ind_j_spice_ship.text: An old nakhuda is selling his ship: a sturdy teak hull sewn with coconut rope, and an experienced crew. With your own ship your pepper and ginger can go to Hormuz without middlemen.
ev.ind_j_spice_ship.partner.success: The joint voyage to Aden brought a fine profit.
ev.ind_j_spice_ship.partner.failure: The winds delayed the voyage and prices fell. You barely got your share back.
ev.ind_j_faqir_hermitage.title: The hermitage
ev.ind_j_faqir_hermitage.text: Disciples have gathered around you, and a rich landowner offers to build you a hermitage with a well and a kitchen where every wanderer will get bread. But a hermitage means walls, and you left walls behind.
ev.ind_j_faqir_hermitage.text.islam: Murids have gathered around you, and a rich amir offers to build a khanqah, a Sufi lodge with a kitchen where every traveller will get bread. But a lodge means walls, and you left walls behind.
ev.ind_j_kavi_contest.title: The poetry contest
ev.ind_j_kavi_contest.text: An evening of verse at the palace: each poet must improvise lines on a given line, on the spot, before everyone. The winner is promised a robe of honour and a purse of gold.
ev.ind_j_kavi_contest.compete.success: They were repeating your lines till dawn. Your patron had your mouth filled with sugar, the reward for sweet speech.
ev.ind_j_kavi_contest.compete.failure: The rhyme slipped away and the hall laughed. Your rival recited his verses with evident pleasure.
ev.ind_j_kavi_praise.title: The panegyric
ev.ind_j_kavi_praise.text: Your patron has returned from a campaign in which he burned a defiant city, and he expects a qasida in his praise. You saw the refugees at the gates and do not know what words could glorify such a victory.
ev.ind_j_kavi_praise.veiled: Write verses with a double meaning
ev.ind_j_kavi_praise.veiled.success: The patron heard praise, the connoisseurs heard bitterness. You were rewarded, and in the town people whisper your lines to each other.
ev.ind_j_kavi_praise.veiled.failure: One of your rivals explained the hidden meaning. The patron is furious.
ev.ind_j_qazi_case.title: A case against an amir
ev.ind_j_qazi_case.text: A widowed weaver complains that a powerful amir's men seized her house for a debt that never existed. The amir has sent you a costly gift and a polite letter. Everyone knows what is written between the lines.
ev.ind_j_qazi_case.just.success: You gave the widow back her house. The amir bears a grudge, but the people call you a just qazi.
ev.ind_j_qazi_case.just.failure: The widow got her house back, but a month later, on the amir's complaint, you were removed from office.
ev.ind_j_land_survey.title: Measuring the fields
ev.ind_j_land_survey.text: The treasury has ordered the fields measured afresh and the yield of each recorded over ten years: the tax depends on it. You have been sent with the surveyors. Village headmen offer gifts in return for a "short" rope.
ev.ind_j_land_survey.note: Sher Shah Suri began, and Akbar with his minister Todar Mal completed, the zabt system: fields were measured, ten years of harvests averaged, and tax assessed in cash. The system outlived the Mughals.
ev.ind_j_land_survey.diligent.success: Your lists proved the most accurate in the district. You were taken into the revenue office.
ev.ind_j_land_survey.diligent.failure: There was too much work and you missed the deadline. You were paid, but without praise.
ev.ind_j_sardar.title: The banner
ev.ind_j_sardar.text: In the thick of battle your unit's standard-bearer fell, and the enemy's war elephants are already breaking the ranks. If no one raises the banner, the unit will run.
ev.ind_j_sardar.charge.success: You raised the banner and the unit followed you. After the battle you were made a sardar.
ev.ind_j_sardar.charge.failure: You raised the banner, but an arrow found you first.
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.title: Carving for the temple
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.text: A new temple is being built, and pillars are handed out to the masters for carving: dancers, horses, yali lions, lotus flowers. You are offered a whole row of pillars — do it well and you will be remembered for centuries.
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.text.gujarat: A Jain merchant is building a new temple of white marble, and ceilings and pillars are handed out for carving — lace made of stone. You are offered an entire dome — do it well and you will be remembered for centuries.
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.take.success: The work turned out so well that the priests brought visitors to see it. Now you have your own band of carvers.
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.take.failure: The stone cracked at the hardest spot. You had to start again, and the pay was less.
ev.ind_j_temple_carving.helper: Work as an assistant to the master carver
ev.ind_j_vaidya_court.title: A patient at the palace
ev.ind_j_vaidya_court.text: At night a palanquin was sent for you: a great amir has had a fever for three days, and the court hakims cannot master it. Cure him and you will be showered with gold. Fail and the blame is yours.
ev.ind_j_vaidya_court.treat.success: You found the right remedy, and by morning the fever broke. The amir named you his physician and rewarded you lavishly.
ev.ind_j_vaidya_court.treat.failure: The patient grew worse, and you were thrown out of the palace in disgrace. Lucky that was all.
ev.ind_mv_to_port.title: To the sea
ev.ind_mv_to_port.text: A merchant you know urges you to come to the coast: there cloth and spices go onto ships, and money is made ten times faster than in the capital. "Here you'll be third in line all your life; there you'll be first."
ev.ind_mv_builders_south.title: The City of Victory calls
ev.ind_mv_builders_south.text: They say the rayas of Vijayanagara are building so many temples, palaces and aqueducts that stonecutters and carvers are summoned from all over India and paid in advance. The road south is long and runs through the sultans' lands.
ev.ind_mv_sufi_east.title: The shaykh goes east
ev.ind_mv_sufi_east.text: The Sufi shaykh you have learned from is leaving for Bengal with his disciples, to clear the forest, build a lodge and call people to God. He asks you to come with them.
ev.ind_mv_court_service.title: Service at court
ev.ind_mv_court_service.text: A distant kinsman serving in Delhi writes that the court needs literate, loyal men, and whoever catches the sovereign's eye gets lands and rank. But the capital is far away, and it has its own ways.
ev.ind_f_kabir.title: The weaver's songs
ev.ind_f_kabir.text: An apprentice at the loom hums couplets by Kabir, the weaver of Benares: "If God is in the mosque, whose is the rest of the world? If He is in the stone idol, who knows what is inside?" The mullah and the brahmin frown alike, but people at the bazaar repeat them.
ev.ind_f_kabir.note: Kabir (15th to early 16th century) was a weaver-poet from Varanasi and one of the great saints of the bhakti movement. He mocked the rituals and caste pride of Hindus and Muslims alike, preaching love for the one God. His verses were also included in the Sikh scripture.
ev.ind_f_kabir.tradition: Hold to the faith of your ancestors
ev.ind_f_chaitanya.title: Kirtan
ev.ind_f_chaitanya.text: A kirtan is passing down the street: dozens of people with mridanga drums and little cymbals singing Krishna's names and dancing, lost to everything else. Chaitanya's followers say that before God there are no high or low jatis.
ev.ind_f_chaitanya.note: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534) of Navadvip in Bengal preached love for Krishna through communal singing, sankirtan. His movement accepted people of every caste and even Muslims, and it deeply changed the religious life of Bengal.
ev.ind_f_nanak.title: The Guru's teaching
ev.ind_f_nanak.text: Disciples of Guru Nanak of the Punjab repeat his words: "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim." Their community keeps a common kitchen, the langar, where everyone sits in one row on the ground and eats from one pot, whether brahmin, blacksmith or lord.
ev.ind_f_nanak.note: Guru Nanak (1469–1539) was the founder of Sikhism. He taught one God, honest labour and human equality, rejecting caste distinctions. Under his successors the common kitchen, the langar, became obligatory for all who came to the Guru.
ev.ind_f_nanak.follow: Become a disciple of the Guru
ev.ind_f_nanak.meal: Sit down to the meal with everyone
ev.ind_f_pir.title: The pir
ev.ind_f_pir.text: A pir, a Sufi master, has settled at the forest's edge. With his disciples he clears land for rice, heals the sick, feeds the hungry and speaks of one merciful God. Many of your neighbours already pray with him.
ev.ind_f_pir.note: Islam spread in Bengal largely through Sufi pirs who opened up the forest lands of the delta together with local cultivators. Historians debate exactly how this happened, but by the sixteenth century eastern Bengal had a very large Muslim population.
ev.ind_f_pir.honor: Honour the pir but keep your own faith
ev.ind_f_last_monastery.title: The last monks
ev.ind_f_last_monastery.text: The great monasteries have been ruined, their libraries burned, and the last monks are leaving for the mountains, for Nepal and Tibet. An old monk left you a scroll with a sutra and asked you to remember the Teaching. And the neighbours keep inviting you to festivals at the temple of Vishnu.
ev.ind_f_last_monastery.note: After the raids of the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries the great Buddhist monasteries of Bihar and Bengal — Nalanda, Vikramashila, Odantapuri — fell into decline. Many monks left for Nepal and Tibet, and Buddhism in the Ganges valley gradually faded away.
ev.ind_f_last_monastery.join: Go to the temple with the neighbours
ev.ind_f_paryushan.title: Paryushan
ev.ind_f_paryushan.text: Eight days of the Paryushan fast. The strictest drink only boiled water, and only before sunset, and on the last day everyone asks forgiveness of everyone else: "Micchami dukkadam — may the harm I have done be undone." There is one person you should have asked for forgiveness long ago.
ev.ind_f_paryushan.short: Fast as far as you can
ev.ind_f_mirabai.title: Mira's songs
ev.ind_f_mirabai.text: A wandering singer sings the songs of Mirabai, the Rajput princess who took Krishna as her only husband, left the palace and sang in the streets among the poor. "I danced before Girdhar, and people laughed — let them laugh."
ev.ind_f_mirabai.note: Mirabai (c. 1498 – c. 1547) was a Rajput princess and bhakti poet who devoted her life to love for Krishna. Tradition says she rejected the customs of the royal household and left to wander. Her songs are still sung in India today.
ev.ind_f_raya_muslims.title: The raya's archers
ev.ind_f_raya_muslims.text: The raya is recruiting Muslim mounted archers: he pays well, has given them their own quarter and allowed them to build a mosque. They say a Quran was even placed before the throne, so that in bowing to the raya they would bow to their own book as well.
ev.ind_f_raya_muslims.note: Devaraya II (r. 1424–1446) recruited Muslim horsemen and archers into his army, gave them lands and allowed them to build mosques. A Muslim quarter and mosques existed in Vijayanagara right up to the sack of 1565.
